strengths: The representation engineering approach utilizing the residual stream for reasoning task offers a novel view.
The study is methodologically clear.
The use of models at varying scales and the combination of several metrics (accuracy, KL divergence, entropy) offers a comprehensive evaluation.
The paper clearly explains the steps for deriving control vectors.
The problem of whether reasoning requires distinct treatment than other tasks is important.
This is an insightful technique that can shed light on the behaviour of LLM and reasoning.
Well written.
As far as I am aware, such control vector intervention is a new idea, and the proposed framework for deriving control vectors and their impact (KL div, entropy) is a useful contribution.
The paper explains its methods and findings in a structured and thoughtful way.
The transformer architecture for conceptually reframing this problem is helpful.
I think the result that reasoning is an emergent general information processing ability is useful and important.
The paper provides a clear overview of the motivation and methodology. It is well-structured and self contained.
The paper performs a simple and novel training-free application of an existing method to improve basic capability of LLMs, where it was previously only used for eliciting style modifications.

While other papers have shown that, e.g. truthfulness exists as a direction (or control vector) in representation space, it may still be counterintuitive that a capability such as reasoning is also a “direction” in representation space.
The paper uses auxiliary methods (Entropy & KL divergence) to analyze the results of applying this method.
The paper’s most validating result, as mentioned in the results section: an 8% improvement in the bAbi task over baseline.
It is very clearly presented what the paper wishes to achieve, and the methodology is clear.
The introduction adequately situates this work in the context of prior work in the field.
To the best of my knowledge, the control-vector method has not been tried before on this particular task.
I particularly enjoyed the meticulous introduction that covered the conceptual and mathematical bases for the remainder of the work; it read well as a mini-tutorial on the techniques used here.
weaknesses: The reasoning tasks (IOI and bAbI) used are relatively simple, potentially limiting the conclusions drawn about "reasoning" in general; results might differ on more challenging tasks, and additional experiments on the GSM8K or MATH dataset are requested.

Testing is limited to smaller models (up to 7B parameters), which could restrict applicability of the conclusions; larger models might capture reasoning dynamics differently and the reviewer asks for experiments with Pythia-12B.

The choice of \alpha actually dominates the final outcome, but the paper does not provide a systematic procedure to choose \alpha beforehand; a general routine to determine the value of \alpha and its interpretation is requested.

The paper uses random character strings as "negative" samples and PCA-based control vectors according to empirical performance; the reviewer wonders if the advantage is due to the nature of the IOI task and asks for results on different types of contrastive prompts (e.g., partially correct responses) on GSM8K / MATH to investigate their impact on control vector efficacy.
The Pythia models are only reported for the IOI task; the reviewer requests results of Pythia-1.4B & Pythia-2.8B on the bAbI task as well.

If I understand the figures correctly, there is an apparent decrease for B & BL condition and almost no improvement for A & AL condition with the Pythia-2.8B model in logit-based accuracy, raising doubts about the effectiveness of the approach and the conclusion that there is no intrinsic difference between reasoning and other information‑processing tasks performed by LLMs; further explanation is requested.
Novelty: they apply an existing technique, adapting it to a couple of architectures and deriving prompts pairs for (the work lacks novelty).
The results are only slightly better for some ranges of alpha.
Very few models, very small models, and just two datasets.

The insights about reasoning are somewhat limited; the claim that "reasoning is not necessarily different from any other form of processing done by LLMs" is either a tautology or requires comparison with other specific processing types, and with only two tasks it is limited how much can be extrapolated for understanding reasoning.
The second task (IOI) is too simple, and in some cases, as the authors say, the answer is not fully specified.
The paper only tests the approach on two models; larger models will need to be used to validate these findings.
IOI task is too simple, even though the bABI task is representative; the authors should explore a wider range of reasoning tasks to strengthen the conclusions.
The contrastive approach using random strings seems a bit arbitrary; a more principled method would be more fruitful.
The probability mass results seem to disagree a little with the entropy KL divergence results.

The paper reports a successful application of the method to two datasets, but due to the need for contrastive pairs it requires positive (good reasoning) and negative (bad reasoning) examples, which may be problematic.

The three schemes for generating the “negative” pairs (asking the model to produce an incorrect answer, selecting cases where the model response is not the expected one, selecting a random string of 75 letters) are pointed out as being ‘unnatural’ or not truly negative.
It is unclear from the results how the latter two negative‑pair schemes are tested; the reviewer asks for detailed explanation or an ablation study to understand their effects.

Without analyzing the errors made by the model, it is not entirely obvious that either of these schemes actually push the model towards correct reasoning; clarification is needed on how the different negative examples are weighted or treated and how this impacts the results.

Entropy is expected to decrease as the model veers towards the correct token, which would imply a negative correlation with accuracy, but this does not appear to be the case for Figure 4 (bAbi on Mistral); the entropy appears positively correlated with probability mass, requiring a more detailed analysis.
It feels as if this paper wanted to be about a software tool or framework, but "reasoning" was more attractive as a topic.
Of the four substantive claims concerning reasoning, I don't think a single one is substantiated.

The tasks are reflective of LLM reasoning ability – that is a stretch; IOI is out of the question and bAbI is a toy task, so the claim that this is about "Reasoning" is too heavy for the experimental foundations.

The corresponding task‑representation vectors in the residual stream are appropriately representative of reasoning in LLMs – the paper needs to establish that the tasks chosen are truly reflective of reasoning, which is not currently demonstrated.

The observed increase in task‑performance after applying the method is evidence for an improvement in reasoning as a broad faculty – the reviewer argues that improvement on bAbI alone does not demonstrate a broad reasoning capacity and asks for evidence of generality across substantially different domains.

There is no intrinsic difference between reasoning and other information‑processing tasks as far as an LLM is concerned – the empirical observations are insufficient to substantiate this claim, and the paper’s avoidance of taking a stance on what reasoning is makes the claim hard to evaluate.
